items.title: Study finds AI weather models use 21 times less energy than traditional systems

featured_image.name: Google's new AI model means the outlook for weather forecasting is bright -  Digital Trends

items.description: A pair of developments this week highlight how artificial intelligence is reshaping weather prediction — not only by making it more accessible, but by making it far less energy-intensive. Researchers at the University of California San Diego unveiled Zephyrus, the first AI agent designed to let users query weather and climate data in plain language, while a separate study published in the journal Weather found that AI-driven forecasting models consume at least 21 times less energy than their traditional counterparts over one year of operation.[1]

items.title: IEA proposes largest-ever oil reserve release amid Hormuz crisis

featured_image.name: Tokyo told national oil reserve site to prepare for release ...

items.description:
The International Energy Agency has proposed the largest emergency release of oil reserves in its history, surpassing the 182 million barrels released in two batches during the Russia-Ukraine conflict in 2022, as disruptions to the Strait of Hormuz threaten to upend global energy markets. The proposal, first reported by The Wall Street Journal, was circulated during an extraordinary meeting of IEA member governments on Tuesday, with countries expected to decide by Wednesday — and adoption assured unless even one member objects.[1][2][3]

The move comes as the U.S.-Israel war with Iran, which began with joint strikes on February 28 under Operation Epic Fury, has effectively shut down the world's most critical oil chokepoint. Commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz — which normally carries roughly 20% of global waterborne crude — has ground to a near halt, with maritime intelligence firm Windward reporting just two outbound Iranian-flagged transits and no inbound crossings on March 8.[4][5]

items.title: Jurists accuse Bukele's government of crimes against humanity

featured_image.name: El Salvador likely committed crimes against humanity during state of  emergency, jurists say | Reuters

items.description:
A group of international legal experts filed a formal complaint with the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights on Tuesday, accusing El Salvador's government of committing crimes against humanity during its four-year state of emergency. The 275-page report represents the most serious accusation of human rights violations leveled against President Nayib Bukele's administration since he took office in 2019.[1][2]

The complaint, filed by the International Group of Experts for the Investigation of Human Rights Violations under the State of Exception in El Salvador — known by its Spanish acronym GIPES — alleges there are "reasonable grounds" to conclude that crimes against humanity, as defined by Article 7 of the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court, are taking place in the Central American nation. The report contends that the violations stem from a state policy "known and even promoted by the highest levels of President Nayib Bukele's government."[3][4][1]
